rendered_article:
Viewers keep asking when you’re live next. Give them !schedule, and the bot can answer with your stream times. You make it on Commands in the dashboard: the name connects the message someone types to your reply or chosen actions. Before answering, the bot checks their access and any cooldowns.

Have the bot running, sign in, and select your connected channel in the dashboard. The chat connection must work for the test below; use your connected Twitch chat for this first reply.

Who can use this page

By default, a Moderator, Lead moderator, Editor or Broadcaster can open Commands and change commands. The broadcaster can raise the access requirement.

The broadcaster can also give VIPs list access through Permissions then Actions then Commands. That access is read-only: New command says “You can view this, but your role cannot change it.” The System commands tab is hidden.

Make a useful reply

Start with your stream times in a plain reply. Leave the other options alone until you see that reply in chat.

  1. Open Commands and choose New command. On an empty list, Make the first command opens the same dialog.
  2. Enter schedule in Name.
  3. Keep What it does at Sends a reply, and write your times in Reply. For example: Tuesdays at 19:00 Amsterdam time.
  4. Keep Send the reply to at Twitch chat, Prefix at Channel default, and Match at Starts with.

Type !schedule in your channel’s Twitch chat as the broadcaster or a platform moderator. If your channel uses something other than ! before command names, type that instead. Those accounts can test while you’re offline. An ordinary viewer needs the stream to be live, or Keep commands and rewards on while offline switched on, as well as permission to use the command and no active cooldown. The bot posts Tuesdays at 19:00 Amsterdam time. if you used the example reply.

Your first command is the shorter starting guide when you need only one plain reply. The Channel commands tab holds the commands you make; System commands holds the bot’s own built-in commands.

Rules for the name

Enter the name without the characters chat types before it. The dialog removes spaces at the ends, strips all leading ! characters and makes the name lowercase, so !!Hello becomes hello.

If the name…What happens
is emptyThe dialog says “Give the command a name.”
has whitespace inside itThe bot refuses it: it cannot match a single chat word.
is only the prefixThe bot refuses it: the prefix is added when the command runs.
is already used by another channel commandThe bot refuses it, comparing names without letter case.
is longer than 100 charactersThe bot refuses it.

A refusal leaves the dialog open with the reason in red. Nothing is created.

Edit a command

To update your stream times, open schedule in the list and change Reply. The footer counts your edits, for example “1 unsaved change”. Choose Save changes: the count disappears and the save button turns off. Type the command in chat again to see the new saved times.

The same save applies to the other fields below. Discard restores every field to its saved value. If the bot refuses a save, the reason appears in red and your edits stay in the form.

SettingWhen to change itStarting value for a new command
Who can use itRestrict the command to a role or anyone above it.Everyone
Send the reply toChoose Twitch chat, Chat overlay, Both or Nowhere for a text or random reply.Twitch chat
Read it aloudRequest speech for a text or random reply.Off
Trigger and cooldownsChange the message that runs the command, or how long chat and each person wait between uses.Both cooldowns are 0 seconds; the heading says “No cooldown”.

The chat overlay is a browser source: a web page layer loaded in your streaming app. It shows the reply on stream as a bot line.

Send the reply to is available while creating a text or random reply and when editing it. Read it aloud is in the editor. Neither control shows for a pipeline or code script, which sends and speaks through its own steps.

For a text or random reply, speech is queued only after the reply is successfully sent to chat. Chat overlay alone and Nowhere therefore produce no speech, even with Read it aloud on. The channel’s text-to-speech setup also needs to be ready. Use Cooldowns and permissions to choose access and waits.

Reset a command to its preset

A preset is a ready-made command the bot added to the channel. Only a command from a preset has Reset to preset in the footer. Its dialog lists the settings that will return to the preset and warns “Your edits to them are lost.”

If nothing differs, it says “This command already matches its preset. Resetting changes nothing.” This restores a channel command’s preset; system commands have their own reset controls.

What a command does

A text reply is enough for information such as your schedule or a community link. Reaction in the editor changes the response you first chose under What it does. New commands start with Text unless you choose another response in the creation dialog.

Choose a different response

What you needWhat it does in the dialogReaction in the editorWhat to fill in
One answerSends a replyTextReply, the line the bot sends.
VarietySends a random replyRandom replyReply 1, Reply 2 and so on, with one answer per box.
Several actionsRuns a pipelinePipelinePipeline: choose a pipeline with its own reply step.
An optional response written in codeRuns a code scriptCode scriptScript: choose a script from Scripts. See Scripts (Draft).

Have a suitable pipeline or script ready when choosing that response. Text and random replies go to Twitch chat by default, in the channel’s one bot voice; Send the reply to changes their destination. When your list has no commands, it says “No commands yet.”

Write a reply

You can keep the answer current without editing it every time. Helpers insert information when the command runs; for example:

Welcome! Today we play {stream.game}.

If your current game is Example Game, chat sees “Welcome! Today we play Example Game.” The reply box holds up to 500 characters. An unknown helper produces “Not a known helper here:” under the box, followed by the unknown names. Find the available helpers on Variables and templates.

Write random replies

With Reaction set to Random reply, the bot picks an answer from your list each time someone uses the command.

  1. Choose Edit replies. The Random replies dialog says “One reply per line. The bot picks one of them each time.”
  2. Enter an answer in each numbered box. Add a reply adds another box.
  3. Choose Use these replies. The editor shows the count, for example “3 replies”.
  4. Choose Save changes. The unsaved count disappears and the save button turns off.

The X beside a box removes it; the last box’s X is disabled. A pick list is a separate list that several commands can share.

Start from another command’s replies

Under Or start from a list you already have, the Random replies dialog lists your other random-reply commands. Choose Use the replies of !name to copy its list. The two commands then hold separate copies: editing one does not change the other.

Triggers

The trigger is the message that runs your command. Prefix chooses what goes before its name; Match chooses where that name may appear in the message. Both controls are in the New command dialog and the editor’s Trigger and cooldowns group.

Prefix

The channel’s usual prefix is Command prefix on Bot basics, described on Bot basics and personality.

Prefix choiceWhat chat types
Channel defaultThe channel prefix followed by the name. This is the default, and uses ! if the channel has set none.
CustomThe text you enter in Custom prefix, followed by the name. It needs nonempty text, up to 8 characters.
NoneThe name on its own.

Match

Matching ignores letter case.

Match choiceWhen the command runs
Starts withThe message begins with the prefix and name, followed by whitespace or the end of the message. This is the default. Any trailing text is passed to the command as its input.
ExactThe message is just the prefix and name.
ContainsThe prefix and name appear as a whole word anywhere. A command named cat with no prefix does not run on “category”.
RegexRegex pattern, a text pattern you supply, finds a match in the message text. Choosing this mode does not require the pattern to match the entire message.

Regex needs a pattern. If it is missing, or Custom has no prefix text, creation stops with “Fill in the custom prefix or the regex pattern you picked.” Nothing is created. In the editor, the same missing field keeps Save changes disabled.

Switch a command on or off

Use the switch in its list row or Enabled at the top of its editor. Both save immediately, without Save changes. A command that is off stays listed with Off and answers nobody.

The bot can refuse to switch a command off while something else still runs it. Move or remove those uses first, just as you must before deleting it.

Copy a command

Open a command and choose Duplicate in the footer. A copy of its saved settings opens with -copy after the name, for example !hello-copy.

The copy starts off, so switch it on before testing. Most settings are copied, including Read it aloud, but aliases, preset identity, reply destination and enabled state are not. Aliases are additional names for the original command. The copy has no Reset to preset button and its reply goes to Twitch chat; you only need to choose a destination if you want a different one. Speech still needs successful chat delivery and a ready TTS setup.

If that copy name already exists, the bot refuses the copy and the editor shows the reason.

Delete a command

  1. Open the command and choose Delete in the footer.
  2. In “Delete !name?”, check that you want it removed for good: “Chat can no longer use it.”
  3. Choose Delete command. The editor closes and the command leaves the list.

If something else still runs the command, the confirmation does not open. The editor names each kind of use, its count and up to five names. For example: “Still used by 2 timers: …. Move or remove these first, then delete the command.”

Kind named in the messageWhere to look
rewards: channel-point rewards that run the commandChannel points
timers: scheduled posts, and chat triggersTriggers and timers
event responses: actions for a follow, sub or raidEvent responses
giveawaysGiveaways
catalog itemsEconomy

An other places line can include pending scheduled tasks that run the command. Those uses also block deletion or switching the command off; resolve them before retrying.

Commands that repeat a system command

A channel command can have the same name as a system command. Its row says Repeats !name, and the line above the list counts those commands. When the channel command’s trigger matches, it answers instead of the ordinary system command.

!permit, !unpermit, !mydata, !gdpr and !forgetme always use the system command instead.

To remove all the channel copies, choose Move copies to system, then confirm with Remove copies. This permanently removes those channel commands. An ordinary system command’s saved enabled state, access requirement and cooldowns still apply; removing a copy alone does not guarantee an answer in chat.

Troubleshooting

When something is not right

The command does nothing in chat. Check these in order, with the bot running and connected to the selected channel:

  1. The command’s switch. Off answers nobody.
  2. Who can use it. The viewer needs that role or a higher one.
  3. Prefix and Match. They must fit the message typed; see Triggers.
  4. Send the reply to. Chat overlay and Nowhere send nothing to Twitch chat.
  5. Chat cooldown and Per-person cooldown. Platform broadcasters and moderators bypass these waits; ordinary viewers do not.
  6. Whether the stream is offline. Ordinary viewers’ commands are ignored unless Keep commands and rewards on while offline is on in Bot basics. The platform broadcaster and moderators can still test.

If you changed the reply after creating it, choose Save changes before trying again.
